title: {{NAME}} and the Bone That Shouldn't Exist
moral: Honest curiosity, even when it overturns what you thought you knew, is the greatest scientific gift.

pages.content: The Redstone Badlands were the colour of dried blood and old fire, a maze of eroded gullies and towering hoodoos where the wind carved strange music from the rock. {{NAME}} loved it with his whole heart. He was the youngest member of Dr Priya Okafor's palaeontology field team, officially listed as 'Junior Excavation Assistant,' which meant he carried the brushes, numbered the grid squares, and dreamed of being the one to find something world-changing. The dig site hummed with quiet industry. Two senior excavators, Marcus and Selin, worked a triceratops quarry on the upper ridge, their small hammers tapping like clockwork. Dr Okafor moved between them with her magnifying glass and her calm, brilliant attention. {{NAME}} had been assigned the lower gully, a section everyone agreed was probably empty. He did not mind. He liked the solitude and the stillness, and the way the late sun turned the rock faces into pages of an ancient, unreadable book.

pages.content: He almost missed it. A curve of dark grey, barely the width of his thumb, barely protruding from the mudstone wall, right at eye level in the shaded base of the gully. Most people would have taken it for a root trace or a mineral streak. But {{NAME}} had spent two summers studying bone textures, and the moment his brush touched it he knew. The surface was spongy, porous, laced with the fine honeycomb structure that only fossilised bone possessed. He worked for an hour with his finest brush, uncovering a shape that made his stomach do a slow, dizzying turn. He called Dr Okafor. She arrived, crouched, peered, and then went very, very still, in the way she only did when something truly extraordinary was happening. She looked up at {{NAME}} with an expression caught between delight and disbelief. 'Do you know what formation this layer is?' she asked. '{{NAME}}, if I'm reading this correctly, this bone is forty million years older than it has any right to be.'

pages.content: Word spread fast. Marcus and Selin scrambled down from the ridge. Equipment cases were hauled over. Dr Okafor radioed the university and the connection crackled with barely contained excitement from the other end. {{NAME}} was at the centre of it all, leading the careful excavation, calling out measurements, recording each newly revealed centimetre in his field notebook with a precision that made Dr Okafor nod approvingly. The bone was enormous, far larger than its small beginning had suggested, curving up through the rock like a great dark parenthesis. As Marcus and Selin cleared the surrounding matrix with tiny pneumatic tools, a shape emerged that none of them had expected: a skull, long and narrow, with a crest of bone rising from its crown in a shape no known dinosaur possessed. The team worked in near silence, communicating in glances and sharp intakes of breath. The sun descended. Nobody suggested stopping for dinner. {{NAME}}'s arms ached and his knees were bruised from the rocky ground, and he had never been happier in his life.

pages.content: The hardest moment came after the discovery, not during it. Late that evening, a professor from the university called back with a sharp voice and a sharp theory: the bone must be contamination, a misidentified fragment from a different layer, an error in stratigraphy. It happened, he said. It happened to everyone. It had not happened here, and {{NAME}} knew it. He had measured the layer himself, three times, with three different instruments. But the professor was famous and confident and loud, and for a moment {{NAME}} felt the horrible, creeping temptation to agree, to let someone else's certainty replace his own uncomfortable truth. He looked at his notebook. He looked at the photographs. He looked at Dr Okafor, who was watching him quietly, waiting. {{NAME}} straightened his spine and said, clearly and carefully, 'With respect, I would like to walk you through the measurements.' There was a long silence on the radio. Then the professor said, 'Alright. I'm listening.' Dr Okafor exhaled slowly and gave {{NAME}} a single, decisive nod.

pages.content: {{NAME}} lay in his narrow camp bed that night listening to the badlands cool and settle around him, the tent canvas breathing softly in the breeze. Every muscle in his body had earned its tiredness. The fossil would take months to study properly, maybe years, and there were arguments still to be had and measurements still to be verified, but the bone was real and the discovery was real and nothing could change that. He thought about how the gully had looked when he first arrived, how ordinary and empty it seemed, and how the most extraordinary things in the world had a way of hiding in plain sight until someone decided to look carefully. His eyes closed, slow and warm, and the red rocks outside seemed to glow faintly in the starlight like embers of the ancient world. He was nearly asleep when he heard it, a sound from somewhere deep in the eastern gully, rhythmic and low, like something vast and slow was breathing in the dark just beyond the circle of the camp lights.
